claims.text: Mechanical-property variations among equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its quaternary and ternary subsets are governed by the degree of short-range chemical order.
Short-range chemical order alters local dislocation pinning.
Short-range chemical ordering or clustering can occur in concentrated Cr-Co-Fe-Ni-based alloys.
Controlled annealing can enhance short-range order in equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni.
Enhancing short-range order increases yield strength.
Enhancing short-range order modifies strain-hardening behavior.
Slow cooling after annealing at 600–800 °C promotes short-range chemical clustering.
Rapid quenching after annealing at 600–800 °C suppresses short-range chemical clustering.
Ordered local chemical environments act as effective pinning sites for dislocations.
Dislocation pinning by ordered chemical environments increases the energy barriers for dislocation motion.
Reducing short-range order reduces obstacles to dislocation motion.
Slow-cooled specimens will have higher yield strength than the conventionally processed equiatomic quinary baseline.
Rapidly quenched specimens will have lower yield strength than the conventionally processed equiatomic quinary baseline.
Changes in short-range order will alter ductility or failure mode.
Annealing at or above approximately 600 °C can induce precipitation or phase transformations in related Cr-Co-Fe-Ni-based alloys.
Annealing-induced precipitates or phase transformations can confound attribution of mechanical-property changes to short-range order.
High-resolution TEM and diffraction can quantitatively distinguish the short-range-order states created by the proposed cooling treatments.
The proposed mechanism is limited to single-phase FCC alloys annealed at 600–800 °C and deformed at room temperature.
